title: Mastering Unit & Integration Testing in Java

cards.title: Introduction to JUnit 5 Lifecycle
cards.content:
JUnit 5 is the modern testing standard for Java applications. It is split into three sub-projects: JUnit Platform, JUnit Jupiter, and JUnit Vintage.

Understanding the test lifecycle annotations is key to writing clean tests:

  • @BeforeAll: Runs once before all test methods in the current class (must be static).
  • @BeforeEach: Runs before every individual @Test.
  • @AfterEach: Runs after every individual @Test.
  • @AfterAll: Runs once after all tests have executed (must be static).
@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_METHOD)
class OrderServiceTest {
    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        // Initialize fresh test fixtures
    }
}

cards.title: Advanced Assertions in JUnit 5
cards.content:
JUnit Jupiter offers rich assertion mechanisms that improve upon standard structural assertions.

1. Grouped Assertions

Using assertAll(), all assertions within the block are executed even if one or more fail. This provides a complete picture of failures in a single run.

assertAll("Address assertion",
    () -> assertEquals("Prague", address.getCity()),
    () -> assertEquals("Czechia", address.getCountry())
);

2. Exception Testing

Use assertThrows() to verify if a block of code throws a specific exception.

IllegalArgumentException exception = assertThrows(
    IllegalArgumentException.class, 
    () -> calculator.divide(10, 0)
);
assertEquals("Cannot divide by zero", exception.getMessage());

content.text:
Complete the test block to catch an empty payload execution exception:

assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> userService.saveUser([blank]));

cards.title: Mocking with Mockito
cards.content:
Mockito allows isolated unit testing of classes by mocking their outer dependencies. This ensures fast execution and zero side effects (e.g., bypassing live database/network calls).

Stubbing

Configure a method call on a mock instance to return a predefined value using when().thenReturn().

when(paymentClient.charge(100.00)).thenReturn(new ChargeResult(Status.SUCCESS));

Verification

Assert that a mock method was actually invoked with specific arguments using verify().

verify(notificationService, times(1)).sendEmail(eq("user@test.com"), anyString());

cards.title: Integration Testing & Spring Slices
cards.content:
While @SpringBootTest bootstraps the entire ApplicationContext, specialized Test Slices load only the minimum component layers required, saving startup time:

  • @WebMvcTest: Focuses only on Spring MVC controllers, security configurations, and filters. Dependencies must be loaded via @MockBean.
  • @DataJpaTest: Configures an in-memory database, configures Hibernate, and scans only @Entity classes and JPA repositories. Transactions auto-rollback at the end of each test method.
@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)
class UserControllerTest {
    @Autowired
    private MockMvc mockMvc;

    @MockBean
    private UserService userService;
}

items.text: Arrange: Set up mocks, environment variables, and prepare input arguments.
Act: Invoke the exact target method being unit-tested.
Assert: Validate returned results and verify dependencies' interactions.
Teardown: Release shared resources (handled automatically or inside @AfterEach).

cards.title: Test-Driven Development (TDD)
cards.content:
TDD changes developer mindset from "writing code, then checking it" to "using tests to design software architecture."

The canonical cycle consists of three steps:

  1. Red: Write a failing test for a piece of missing functionality. The test must fail to compile or assert negative behavior.
  2. Green: Write the minimum amount of functional code necessary to make the test pass successfully.
  3. Refactor: Clean up both business logic code and test structures (reducing duplication, fixing style issues) without changing the overall behavior.

options.text: Refactoring your code base while tests are failing (Red phase).
Writing the minimal, simplest code possible to pass a test, even if it uses a hardcoded return value.
Skipping the failing test phase if you already know the architectural design perfectly.
Writing all system-wide integrations and mocks first before defining unit tests.
